analysis.one_liner: Lets hourly workers request schedule changes and requires two weeks' notice, with extra pay for last-minute changes.
analysis.headline: The bill died without any committee or floor vote when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, after drawing 37 cosponsors — every one a Democrat.
analysis.plain_summary: The Schedules That Work Act would have given hourly workers a protected right to ask for schedule changes and required employers to negotiate in good faith. For retail, food service, cleaning, hospitality, and warehouse workers, it would have required work schedules two weeks in advance, extra pay for last-minute changes and split shifts, and at least 11 hours of rest between shifts, with back pay and lawsuit rights for violations. It never received a vote in any committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly, non-exempt workers at companies with 15 or more employees, especially in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses — jobs the bill's findings say are filled disproportionately by low-paid women and workers of color. They would gain schedules posted 14 days ahead, an estimate of their minimum monthly hours, extra pay when employers change schedules late or cut posted hours, an extra hour of pay for split shifts, the right to decline shifts starting less than 11 hours after their last one, protection from retaliation for asking, and the ability to sue for owed pay plus equal liquidated damages [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food, hotel, and warehouse workers

how_it_helps.text: Gives every covered employee the right to request changes to hours, shift times, work location, advance notice, and hour fluctuations, and requires the employer to discuss the request in good faith; requests tied to caregiving, serious health conditions, training, or a second job must be granted unless the employer has a bona fide business reason to refuse

Requires retail, food service, cleaning, hospitality, and warehouse employers to hand workers their schedules at least 14 days ahead, with $75 per day in pay for each day a schedule is not provided, plus a written estimate of minimum monthly hours for the next year

Requires 'predictability pay' — one extra hour of wages when the employer adds hours or moves a shift with less than 14 days' notice, and at least half-time pay for every scheduled hour the employer cancels

Pays workers an extra hour for split shifts and lets them decline any shift starting less than 11 hours after the last one ended — the 'clopening' pattern — unless they consent in writing and are paid 1.5 times their rate

Makes retaliation for requesting changes or filing complaints unlawful, and enforces the rules through Department of Labor investigations and private lawsuits with double (liquidated) damages, interest, and attorney's fees

Targets a documented problem: the bill's findings cite survey data that about two-thirds of hourly retail and food service workers get less than two weeks' notice of schedules, one in five work on-call shifts, one in three work clopening shifts, and 65% want more stable schedules

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses. They would bear direct labor costs — $75 per day for missed notice, extra hours of pay for late changes and split shifts, 1.5x pay for short-turnaround shifts — plus recordkeeping, written-consent tracking, and scheduling-system costs, and they would lose the flexibility to post schedules on short notice or cancel shifts without paying for them [S3]. Some of those costs would likely reach consumers through prices and some could come back to workers through tighter staffing or hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: The notice, predictability, and split-shift pay mandates are real labor costs for low-margin employers, and the $75-per-day penalty accrues per employee per day, so costs would fall hardest on chain restaurants, retailers, and franchisees and could surface as higher prices, tighter hours, or pressure to automate scheduling-heavy jobs

For most requests — anything not tied to caregiving, health, training, or a second job — the employer may deny 'for any reason that is not lawful,' so the headline right-to-request is only a right to an answer with a stated reason, not a right to a change
Unionized workers can be excluded entirely if their collective bargaining agreement covers scheduling and expressly waives the act, a carve-out labor groups often criticize in bills like this

Employers owe no predictability pay for worker-requested changes, agreed shift trades, utility failures, natural disasters, declared emergencies, or severe weather, and the good-faith exception lets courts waive double damages for reasonable-cause violations — softening both the worker protections and the employer incentives

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are concrete and targeted: advance notice, minimum-hours estimates, and premium pay directly address income instability that makes child care, second jobs, and benefit eligibility hard to hold together. For employers, the costs are real but structured — premium pay applies only to employer-initiated late changes, penalties are capped per violation, and states and cities have operated similar predictive-scheduling rules. The design is uneven, though: the right-to-request provision has little teeth for most workers, the collective-bargaining waiver leaves out union members, and the largest cost pressures land on small franchisees rather than the large chains whose scheduling practices drove the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House committees from February 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023 — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro and 23 colleagues introduced the bill on February 9, 2022, and it was immediately referred to four committees — Education and Labor, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Judiciary — splitting jurisdiction among them
The bill attracted 37 cosponsors by the end, every one a House Democrat; no Republican signed on

On November 1, 2022, the Judiciary referral was sent one level down to its Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee — the only movement the bill ever got after its introduction-day referral
None of the four committees ever held a markup or voted on the bill, the House never took it up, and all pending legislation died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers — and the large chains whose just-in-time scheduling practices the bill targeted — are better off, because they never had to absorb the 14-day notice, predictability pay, split-shift pay, or rest-period mandates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were House Democrats and none of the bill's provisions ever reached a recorded vote, so support was entirely one-party while opposition never had to show itself on a tally.

industries.note: The industries with the worst just-in-time scheduling would owe $75 a day for late schedules, premium pay for late changes and split shifts, and 1.5x pay for clopening shifts — a direct hit to the labor-cost flexibility their business models rely on. Workers in these jobs would gain predictable pay and notice.

Retail employers would have to post schedules 14 days ahead, estimate minimum monthly hours a year out, and pay for every cancelled posted hour — ending the practice of adjusting staffing on short notice at no cost. The bill's own findings cite retail scheduling practices as a core target.

Hospitality establishments are explicitly covered by the notice, predictability-pay, split-shift, and rest-period requirements, which touch housekeeping and front-desk scheduling patterns built around variable occupancy.

Warehouse establishments are named in the notice and pay mandates, aimed at volatile peak-season scheduling at large fulfillment operations. Workers there would gain minimum-hours estimates and pay for cancelled shifts.
Cleaning occupations are explicitly covered, and split-shift and short-notice premiums land on firms that schedule crews around building hours, often with fragmented shifts.

Employers would need systems to post schedules electronically, track written consent for off-schedule and short-rest shifts, and itemize premium pay on pay stubs — a compliance market for scheduling-software providers.
